It's a little complicated. CHIPS is a netting network, so it settles transactions at end-of-business by netting credits and debits, and then transferring funds from one bank's account to another (fedwire is near-realtime money transfer). Bank A wires $500k to Bank B and later that day Bank B wires $1MM to Bank A. If sent over chips, no money transfers until the end of the day, when the network transfers $500k from Bank B to Bank A (the net transaction). If sent over fedwire, two separate transactions actually occur.

But according to the UCC-4A, an accountholder gets the money as soon as the wire notice arrives. The second the bank credits money to the destination account, the transfer is complete and final and there is no recourse against the accountholder by the bank. With fedwire, this is fine, there's no risk of loss in the system because the money is credited to the destination bank's account with the fed simultaneously with the wire being received by the bank (and the transfer system is considered risk free, as it's backed by the full faith and credit of the US Government).

With CHIPS there's a slight risk of loss in the system, because the recipient bank doesn't actually receive the money until the day's netting is complete, and there is a slight risk of systemic loss (the CHIPS network itself going bankrupt). To make up for this, the costs for CHIPS transfers are less than fedwire, and the owners/members only allow banks they believe strong enough into the system.

As an accountholder, there's generally little to no difference. I've seen wires go faster through CHIPS than fedwire, and vice versa, and there doesn't seem to be any rhyme or reason to which one a bank chooses. I haven't seen any cheaper fees for CHIPS, so I assume it's a marginal profit thing.https://www.fatwallet.com/forums/finance/987407﻿
